reading.rtitle: The Sisters at the Window -- Clara Whitfield, 1889
paras: The painting in front of you is called The Sisters at the Window. It was made by Clara Whitfield, an American artist who was born in Baltimore in 1861 and who spent most of her life within thirty miles of this building. The canvas depicts two young women who are sitting at a kitchen window on a winter afternoon. The window, which takes up almost half of the picture, looks out on a landscape of flat fields and one grey road. Whitfield is known above all for her portraits, and this is the only work in which she puts a portrait and a landscape inside the same frame.

The painting was a commission. In 1889 a family who owned a mill outside Washington asked Whitfield to paint their two daughters, and they paid her ninety dollars, which was more than a teacher earned in half a year. The letter in the case to your right, where the price is written in pencil, is the only document we have from that exchange. The family expected a formal portrait of two girls in good dresses. What they received was this: two sisters who are looking away from the painter, in a room where almost nothing has been arranged for the viewer. The mill owner never hung it. It stayed in a corridor for forty years.

Now look at the color. The first rooms of this exhibit are full of loud work: red curtains, blue dresses, skies that seem to shout at you. The Sisters at the Window belongs to the era that came after, when Whitfield turned to a muted range of grey, sand and a faded green. Only one thing in the picture is striking, and it is very small: the orange of a cup on the table, which the eye finds again and again. Visitors often ask whether the painting has faded with time. It has not. The brushstrokes tell you it was always quiet -- thin, careful, and almost invisible at the edges.

The canvas was restored in 1998, and the work took eleven months. Under the surface the restorers found a third figure, a woman who is standing in the doorway behind the sisters, and whom Whitfield had painted over herself. Nobody knows who she was. The X-ray photograph on the wall to your left, where you can see her clearly, was made during that year. The painting belongs to a museum in Baltimore and is here on loan until March, together with four other works from the same era. After that it goes home, and this wall will hold a landscape that has not been shown in public since 1954.

listenings.text: Stop number four. You are standing in front of The Sisters at the Window, and I would like you to do three things. First, step back about two meters. From there the canvas reads as one grey block with a single orange point in the middle, which is the cup on the table, and that cup is the reason the whole picture holds together. Now walk in as close as the rope allows. From here you can see every brushstroke on the girls' hands, and you will notice that the hands are the only part of the painting that was finished twice. Finally, look at the doorway behind them, on the right. There is a shape there that most visitors walk straight past, and it is not a shadow. It is a woman who was painted over by the artist, and who came back in 1998, when the canvas was restored. Hold that thought, and turn to your left.

Good morning, and welcome to the museum. The galleries are open today from ten until five thirty, and the last entry is at four forty-five. Please note that the special exhibit on the third floor, American Painting Before the War, closes this Sunday, so if you have come for that one, we suggest you start upstairs. Photography without flash is allowed in all of our permanent rooms. It is not allowed in the third-floor exhibit, because several of those works are on loan from other collections, and their owners do not permit it. Large bags, backpacks and umbrellas must be left at the coat check, which you will find behind the ticket desk on your right, next to the elevators. That service is free of charge. Enjoy your visit, and if you need anything at all, our staff wear a blue badge.

I think people find museums exhausting for a very simple reason, and the reason is not the art. It is that they walk in and try to look at everything, you know, four hundred works in two hours, and by the third room the brain has just closed the door. I mean, nobody would sit down and read forty books in an afternoon. So here is what I do, and I have done it for years now. I pick three. Three works, and I let the rest go. I walk the whole floor quickly, almost rudely, and I choose one portrait, one landscape, and one thing that simply looks striking to me, and then I go back and I stay with each one for ten minutes. Ten minutes in front of a painting is a very long time, and something always happens in the last two.
